newsitem.title: USA: Summit to widen New Jersey lead with merger.
newsitem.headline: Summit to widen New Jersey lead with merger.

text.p: Summit Bancorp, New Jersey's largest bank based on in-state deposits, has widened its lead with the planned acquisition of Collective Bancorp Inc and at the same time enhanced its own appeal as a takeover candidate.
"In my opinion it makes them that much more attractive," said Robert Bonelli, executive vice president and chief financial officer at Ernst & Co.
The acquisition would boost Summit's market share in New Jersey to 16.1 percent from 13.4 percent.
Bonelli said the $867 million deal would add to Summit's earnings in the first full year.

"This is definitely a positive for Summit. I like the transaction and I think it's perfectly in line with their strategy of making themselves the premier player in the New Jersey-Pennsylvania marketplace," he said.

"If I were an acquirer, say NationsBank Corp coming up from the South or someone coming from the Midwest, and I wanted to have a New Jersey-Pennsylvania presence, beyond any shadow of a doubt it's Summit," Bonelli continued.
Asked if Summit, as a result of the Collective deal, had enhanced its own attractiveness as a takeover candidate, Salomon Brothers analyst Michael Plodwick said, "One would think so."
"it looks like the best franchise available in the region," he said.

Asked to comment on Summit's strategy amid a wave of banking industry consolidation, Summit spokeswoman Barbara Horn said, "Our acquisition strategy has been and continues to be to pursue in-market acquisitions that will enhance our franchise."
She said Summit's policy is not to comment on rumors or speculation about particular deals.

Plodwick said he reiterated a buy rating on Summit and kept his 1997 and 1998 earnings projections at $3.60 per share and $4.00, respectively. He said there could be "a little upside" to the 1998 estimate.

Elizabeth Summers, analyst at Ryan, Beck & Co, said a Summit projection that it expected to save about $18 million a year, or 25 percent of Collective's annual expense base, appeared to be a conservative figure.
"It appears to be very low for an in-market acquisition," she said.
Asked about possible layoffs, Horn said a 20-25 percent saving in employee-related expenses was anticipated.

Horn also said the Summit organization currently has about 400 job openings, including mid-management positions. The company plans to open 70 branches inside supermarkets in the next 18 months, she said.
Summit was formed when Princeton, N.J.-based UJB Financial Corp acquired a New Jersey bank known as Summit in early 1996 and took the Summit name.
Summit has 70 branches in eastern Pennsylvania, and loan production and discount brokerage operations in New York and Connecticut.

Ranked by in-state deposits, Summit is the largest bank in New Jersey. The next four largest are all headquartered outside the state: Charlotte, N.C.-based First Union Corp ; Pittsburgh-based PNC Bank Corp ; Boston-based Fleet Financial Group Inc, and Philadelphia-based CoreStates Financial Corp.
Summit was up 1/8 to 47-5/8 in afternoon trading, while Collective was off 1-1/8 to 40-7/8.
The decline in Collective was due in part to a run-up in the price prior to a deal, analysts said.
